assessments.explanation: The abstract reports an overall prevalence of abnormal prion protein in archived UK appendix samples of 493 per million population (95% CI 282 to 801 per million) and concludes this suggests a high prevalence of infection indicating vCJD carrier status. It never states an absolute count of carriers, so it neither confirms nor refutes the figure of 1,000. The reported rate would imply a far larger number for the UK population, but that requires population figures not in the abstract, so the claim cannot be assessed directly from this abstract.

This research letter describes a single preclinical vCJD case, in which a transfusion recipient had prion protein in spleen and lymph node tissue, and says the findings have major implications for future estimates of vCJD in the UK. It gives no estimate of the number of asymptomatic carriers in the UK, so it does not address the claim of 1,000 carriers.

This research letter reports a single preclinical vCJD case (a blood transfusion recipient who died of a non-neurological disorder, with prion protein detected in spleen and a lymph node). It says the findings have 'major implications for future estimates and surveillance of vCJD in the UK' but gives no population count or prevalence estimate, so it neither supports nor refutes 1,000 asymptomatic carriers.

This survey of 32,441 archived UK appendix samples found abnormal PrP in 16 samples, an overall prevalence of 493 per million population (95% CI 282 to 801 per million). The authors conclude this 'suggests a high prevalence of infection with abnormal PrP, indicating vCJD carrier status in the population' compared with 177 clinical cases. The claim of 1,000 carriers is not stated in the abstract. However, applying the reported prevalence to a UK population of roughly 60 million (an external figure not in the abstract) gives on the order of tens of thousands, and 1,000 people corresponds to about 17 per million, below the lower confidence bound of 282. The claimed count is therefore incompatible with the reported prevalence. The study measures abnormal PrP in appendix tissue, so it is an inference that these positives represent asymptomatic vCJD carriers, as the authors themselves state.

The abstract covers youth-to-adult homelessness progression and early intervention, but says nothing about the availability of safe places to study or their effect on homelessness.
The abstract discusses health problems of homeless people and barriers to health care. It does not mention study spaces or their effect on homelessness.
The abstract reviews effects of homelessness on children and policy needs. It does not address safe study places or whether they affect homelessness rates.

assessments.explanation: The abstract (T-ALL, human tumor data plus network analysis) identifies RUNX1 as a tumor suppressor in T cell transformation and reports recurrent somatic loss-of-function RUNX1 mutations in human T-ALL. This runs opposite to the claim that normal RUNX1 expression promotes tumors. It does not directly test normal expression levels, so the contradiction is directional rather than a direct experimental test of the claim.

In gastric cancer cell lines and tissues, RUNX1 is described as a tumor suppressor. miR-675 (induced by H19) targets RUNX1, and RUNX1 expression is inversely related to H19/miR-675 in gastric cancer tissues and cell lines. This implies that RUNX1 restrains rather than promotes tumor growth, which is incompatible with the claim. The evidence is mechanistic and correlational in cell lines and tissues, not a direct manipulation of normal RUNX1 expression.

This glioblastoma study examines a broad microRNA-RNA interaction network and reports that RUNX1 is among the genes regulated by it. The abstract does not state the direction of RUNX1's effect on tumor growth or whether normal RUNX1 expression promotes tumors, so it neither supports nor contradicts the claim.

The abstract identifies RUNX1 as a tumor suppressor in T-ALL, predicting a tumor-suppressor role in T cell transformation and reporting recurrent loss-of-function RUNX1 mutations in human T-ALL. This indicates RUNX1 restrains rather than promotes tumorigenesis, contrary to the claim that normal RUNX1 expression promotes tumors. It does not directly test 'normal expression' levels, so the contradiction is indirect.

The abstract describes RUNX1 as a tumor suppressor and shows that RUNX1 is a direct target of miR-675 whose expression is inversely related to H19/miR-675 in gastric cancer tissues and cell lines. RUNX1 thus acts protectively against gastric cancer cell growth, which conflicts with the claim that normal RUNX1 expression is tumor-promoting. The evidence is indirect, as the study does not test normal RUNX1 expression per se.

The abstract reports that CX3CR1 signaling promotes T(H)2 cell survival in inflamed lungs, and that CX3CR1-deficient Th2 cells expressing BCL-2 restore asthma. This is the opposite of the claim that CX3CR1 on Th2 cells impairs their survival.

The claim says CX3CR1 on Th2 cells impairs T cell survival. The abstract, which is a mouse study of allergic airway inflammation, reports the opposite direction: CX3CR1 signaling promoted T(H)2 survival in inflamed lungs, and BCl-2-transduced CX3CR1-deficient T(H)2 cells restored asthma. It also reports CX3CR1-induced survival for T(H)1 cells during airway inflammation, but only under inflammatory conditions. The evidence is from mice and T cells in vivo, so it does not directly address humans. Only one abstract was read, so this is a single-study assessment.

The abstract (Xenopus embryos) reports that ADMP transcription in the Spemann organizer (dorsal) is activated at low BMP levels (sentence 3), and that ADMP has BMP-like activity but is unable to signal dorsally because of inhibition by Chordin (sentence 6). It does not use the term 'activator-inhibitor pair' or describe the Admp/Chordin pair as a dorsal activator-inhibitor system, so the claim's framing is not established. The dorsal Chordin inhibition of ADMP signalling is related but does not directly match the claim, so I return NOT_ENOUGH_INFO rather than CONTRADICT.

The abstract (amphibian embryos) describes Spemann's organizer secreting Chordin, a BMP antagonist (sentence 0), and a Sizzled-Chordin feedback loop that scales dorsal-ventral patterning (sentences 2-4). It does not mention Admp or any activator-inhibitor pair provided dorsally by Admp and Chordin, so it neither supports nor contradicts the claim.

The abstract describes ADMP as a dorsal BMP-like signal (an activator of BMP signaling via ALK-2) that is inhibited dorsally by Chordin. It concludes that dorsal and ventral BMP signals and their extracellular antagonists provide a self-regulation mechanism. This supports the claim that ADMP and Chordin form a dorsal activator-inhibitor pair, though the abstract never uses the term 'activator-inhibitor'.

The abstract covers Chordin as a BMP antagonist secreted by Spemann's organizer and its regulation by Sizzled in DV patterning. It does not mention Admp or describe an activator-inhibitor pair, so it neither supports nor contradicts the claim.

The abstract reports that CX3CR1 is required for airway inflammation. CX3CR1-deficient mice and WT mice given CX3CR1-blocking reagents had reduced lung disease. Transferring WT CD4+ T cells restored asthma features in CX3CR1-deficient mice. CX3CR1 signaling promoted TH2 survival in inflamed lungs. This is the opposite of the claim that CX3CR1 on Th2 cells suppresses airway inflammation.

This is a mouse study (with some human observations). CX3CR1-deficient mice, or WT mice treated with CX3CR1-blocking reagents, showed reduced lung disease after allergen challenge, so CX3CR1 promotes rather than suppresses airway inflammation. Transferring WT CD4+ T cells restored asthma features in CX3CR1-deficient mice, and CX3CR1 signaling promoted TH2 survival in inflamed lungs. The abstract reports the opposite direction of effect from the claim, which says CX3CR1 on Th2 cells suppresses airway inflammation.

Rodent study (aged rodents, mouse model). Sentence 1 states the authors' prior finding that chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA) activity declines in aged organisms; sentence 3 notes the CMA lysosomal receptor decreases in abundance with age. The claim is general ('autophagy'), but the abstract addresses one autophagy pathway (CMA) in aged rodents, so the support is for CMA specifically and is a stated prior finding rather than a result established in this paper. Sentence 5 (CMA maintained at advanced ages when receptor decline is prevented) is consistent with the decline but was not cited as the primary support.

Review of autophagy in stem cell renewal, differentiation, proliferation, and aging. The title mentions aging, but the readable abstract does not report any finding that autophagy declines with age in organisms.
Guidelines for assays monitoring autophagy and distinguishing autophagosome accumulation from autophagic flux. It does not address age-related changes in autophagy.

The study reports that autophagy-related proteins (LC3II/I, Beclin-1, LAMP2) in rat liver decreased significantly with increasing age, and that hepatic autophagic deficiency is associated with aging liver. This directly supports the claim that autophagy declines in aged organisms (in rat liver).
This review covers autophagy in stem cell renewal, differentiation, and proliferation. Its title mentions aging, but the abstract does not report any age-related decline in autophagy.
This C. elegans study examines neurite outgrowth and synaptic decline with age. It does not measure or mention autophagy, so it neither supports nor contradicts the claim.

assessments.explanation: Human cortex study (125 subjects, 17 weeks gestation to 104 years) reporting DNA methylation changes across the lifespan at 50 loci, including neurogenesis-related NEUROD1 and NEUROD2, with age-related methylation increases. These are observational age associations. The study did not modify the epigenome experimentally, so it does not show that epigenomic modification affects human aging through neurogenesis genes. The claim is causal and the abstract is correlational, so it is not sufficient to support or contradict the claim.

Review article arguing that age-dependent changes in transcriptional and chromatin networks contribute to aging in general. It does not address the brain, neurogenesis, or specific neurogenesis-related genes, and it reports no intervention on the brain epigenome. It is too general to support or contradict the specific claim.

Mouse study of hippocampal neural stem cells. It reports that reduced neurogenesis in aged mice correlates with loss of active horizontal NSCs and that the quiescent state is reversible. It does not study epigenetic modification, DNA methylation, or chromatin, and it does not involve human subjects. It does not address the claim's epigenomic mechanism or human aging.

This twin study measured body-mass index (BMI), a proxy for obesity, not obesity itself. Identical twins reared apart had intrapair correlations of 0.70 (men) and 0.66 (women), and heritability estimates were 0.74 (men) and 0.69 (women) by model fitting. The authors conclude that genetic influences are substantial and that childhood environment has little or no influence. Environmental influences unique to the individual contributed about 30 percent of variance. Genetic influence is therefore a major contributor, which is incompatible with obesity being determined solely by environment.

This family study of obese and non-obese children and their relatives in Aosta, Italy, concluded that genetic factors are certainly present in obesity and suggested a dominant major gene with weak effect. Presence of a genetic contribution is incompatible with the claim that obesity is determined solely by environmental factors. The study is a single-population human study and does not quantify the total genetic share.

Identical twins reared apart show a BMI correlation of about 0.66-0.70, with heritability estimates of roughly 0.69-0.74. The authors conclude genetic influences are substantial and childhood environment has little or no influence. Environment contributes about 30% of variance, so obesity is not determined solely by environment.

Adoptee weight class tracks the BMI of biologic parents but not adoptive parents. The authors conclude genetic influences play an important role in determining human fatness, while the family environment alone has no apparent effect. This contradicts the claim that obesity is determined solely by environment.

The abstract states that PTEN and its pseudogene PTENP1 are functionally related through competition for microRNA binding, a protein-coding-independent mechanism. It reports that PTENP1 is biologically active, can regulate cellular levels of PTEN, and exerts a growth-suppressive role, which supports the claim that PTENP1 regulates PTEN expression as a miRNA decoy.

The abstract describes a broad miRNA sponge network in glioblastoma and shows that miR-mediated regulators of PTEN affect PTEN expression. It never mentions PTENP1 or a pseudogene, so it neither supports nor contradicts the specific claim that the PTENP1 pseudogene acts as a miRNA decoy for PTEN.

The abstract proposes that RNAs can compete for microRNA binding independently of coding function, uses the PTEN/PTENP1 pair as its model, and reports that PTENP1 is biologically active because it can regulate cellular levels of PTEN and exert a growth-suppressive role. This supports the claim's core mechanism. It is a cell/tumour-biology study, and the abstract does not explicitly use the phrase 'miRNA decoy'. It frames the mechanism as competition for microRNA binding, which is the same concept.

This glioblastoma study reports miRNA-mediated sponge networks and says that siRNA silencing of 13 miR-mediated PTEN regulators downregulated PTEN. It does not mention the pseudogene PTENP1 or test a pseudogene acting as a miRNA decoy, so it neither supports nor contradicts the pseudogene-specific claim.

This study examines the general ceRNA hypothesis using an miR-122 target in mouse hepatocytes and liver, concluding that modulating miRNA target abundance is unlikely to cause significant ceRNA effects. It does not study PTEN or PTENP1, so its liver-specific, non-PTEN findings do not contradict the claim about PTENP1 regulating PTEN in other contexts.

The abstract is a retrospective before-and-after cohort of 14,786 Canadian patients receiving RBC transfusions, comparing outcomes before and after a universal prestorage leukoreduction program. It reports that serious nosocomial infections did not decrease after leukoreduction (adjusted OR 0.97; 95% CI 0.87-1.09), and that posttransfusion fever and antibiotic use decreased. It does not study leuko-increased blood as an exposure linked to higher infection risk, so it does not establish the claimed increase. The null infection result is weak evidence against the claim, but it is not incompatible with it, so NOT_ENOUGH_INFO is the appropriate verdict. Only one abstract was read, so the claim remains unresolved in this corpus.

The abstract compares a control period (leuko-increased blood) with a period after universal prestorage leukoreduction. The primary outcome, serious nosocomial infections, did not differ (adjusted OR 0.97, 95% CI 0.87-1.09), so there is no evidence that leuko-increased blood increases serious infections. Posttransfusion fever and antibiotic use were lower after leukoreduction, which is the opposite direction of the claim for those secondary outcomes. The abstract is observational and the infection result is a null finding, so the contradiction is partial. Note that the search returned only one relevant abstract, and I read only that one.

The abstract lists insulin among the exposures studied (sentence 4) and reports kidney failure outcomes, but it does not report any association between insulin and severe kidney failure. The only kidney-failure result concerns glitazones and gliptins versus metformin monotherapy (sentence 9). It therefore cannot support or refute the claim that insulin increases the risk of severe kidney failure.

The abstract is an open cohort study of 469,688 primary-care patients with type 2 diabetes. Insulin is one of the listed exposures (sentence 4), but the reported severe kidney failure findings concern glitazones and gliptins versus metformin (sentence 9). No insulin-specific estimate for severe kidney failure is reported, so the claim that insulin increases the risk of severe kidney failure can be neither supported nor contradicted. Two further searches did not return any other abstract addressing insulin and kidney failure, and I did not read those results.

Human EEG study (noise-free conditions, continuous speech) reporting that the cortical representation of the speech envelope (neural entrainment) is enhanced by congruent audiovisual speech, and that entrainment is inhibited when auditory and visual streams are incongruent both temporally and contextually. MEG study of lip-brain coherence showing visual entrainment and that attending visual speech enhances lip-cortex coherence. MEG study of delta-theta phase tracking of naturalistic audiovisual movies. The abstract reports that cortical entrainment to the continuous auditory speech envelope is enhanced by congruent audiovisual speech in noise-free conditions (sentence 6). It also reports that entrainment is inhibited when auditory and visual streams are temporally and contextually incongruent (sentence 8), and that the auditory speech representation is enhanced when the visual signal shares the same timing (sentence 13).

The abstract shows that delta-theta phase in auditory cortex tracks both auditory and visual stimulus dynamics during audiovisual movies. It does not compare congruent with incongruent audiovisual input, so it cannot confirm that entrainment is strengthened by congruence.

The abstract shows that lip movements entrain visual cortex and that attending to visual speech increases lip-brain coherence. It does not test congruent versus incongruent auditory-visual conditions or report auditory entrainment being strengthened by congruence.

This Tn-seq screen of sporulation genes in B. subtilis does not mention clpC in the abstract, and does not report sporulation efficiency for clpC mutants. It cannot confirm or refute the claim.

This study characterizes CtsR as a repressor of the clpC operon and class III heat shock genes, using expression and promoter-binding assays. It does not measure sporulation efficiency in clpC-deficient cells, so it does not address the claim.

This paper examines Clp protein levels, ClpCP-mediated degradation of ClpE, and clp mRNA half-lives under heat stress. It does not report sporulation outcomes for clpC mutants, so it neither supports nor contradicts the claim.

The abstract reports that Aire is inducibly expressed in human and mouse tumor keratinocytes, and that it is required for timely onset of Gli2-induced skin tumorigenesis in mice. The abstract studies AIRE as a thymic regulator of self-antigen expression in thymic epithelial cells and the immune response to melanoma in AIRE-deficient mice and APECED patients. It does not report AIRE expression within skin tumors, so it neither supports nor contradicts the claim.

The abstract reports that Aire is inducibly expressed in human and mouse tumor keratinocytes in a K17-dependent manner and is required for timely onset of Gli2-induced skin tumorigenesis. The abstract studies AIRE's role in thymic expression of melanoma-associated self-antigens and the anti-melanoma immune response. It does not report AIRE expression within skin tumors themselves.
The abstract concerns Aire's effect on thymic TRP-1 expression and immune rejection of melanoma in Aire-deficient mice. It does not measure or report AIRE expression in tumor tissue.

In this retrospective cohort of 141,311 patients with intracerebral hemorrhage (a stroke subtype), prior NOAC (DOAC) use was associated with lower in-hospital mortality than prior warfarin use (adjusted OR 0.75; adjusted risk difference -5.7%). This abstract studies DOAC trough levels and thromboembolic events in atrial fibrillation patients. It does not address stroke patients, in-hospital mortality, or warfarin comparison.

This retrospective cohort study of 141,311 patients with intracerebral hemorrhage (a stroke subtype) in Get With The Guidelines-Stroke hospitals reports that prior NOAC use was associated with lower in-hospital mortality than prior warfarin use (adjusted risk difference -5.7%, AOR 0.75, 97.5% CI 0.69-0.81). The abstract describes H2A.Z nucleosomes flanking a nucleosome-free region that contains the transcription start site in S. cerevisiae. It does not mention N-terminal cleavage or any method comparison showing that N-terminal cleavage increases success in identifying transcription start sites.

The abstract reports mapping transcription start and termination sites in the mouse genome using full-length cDNAs. It does not mention N-terminal cleavage or compare any cleavage-based approach against others, so the claim is neither supported nor contradicted.
This review concerns DNA methylation across genomic contexts, including transcriptional start sites. It does not address N-terminal cleavage or the success of identifying transcription start sites.

The abstract describes HDV RNA-templated transcription by Pol II in vitro and the specificity of transcription start site selection, which depends on RNA secondary structure. The abstract covers Nt(Q)-amidase (Ntaq1) in the N-end rule protein degradation pathway. It says nothing about transcription start sites or whether N-terminal cleavage aids their identification.

The abstract is about DNA methylation across genomic contexts, including transcriptional start sites and CpG islands. It does not discuss N-terminal cleavage or any method for identifying transcription start sites, so it is not relevant to the claim.

In a mouse model, Kras-mutant lung cancers did not respond substantially to the PI3K/mTOR inhibitor alone, but adding the MEK inhibitor ARRY-142886 produced marked synergy in shrinking these tumors. The authors conclude that PI3K-mTOR inhibitors combined with MEK inhibitors may effectively treat KRAS-mutated lung cancers. This is preclinical mouse data, so it supports the claim with that caveat.

This study combines PI3K inhibition with ERK inhibition, not MEK inhibition, in KRAS-mutant pancreatic cancer cell lines. ERK is downstream of MEK, so it is related but does not directly test the MEK inhibitor combination in the claim. It also reports cell-line synergy, not tumor treatment efficacy.

The study tests PI3K inhibitor PX-866 alone in xenografts and finds oncogenic Ras drives resistance to it. It does not test any MEK inhibitor combination, so it neither supports nor contradicts the claim about combined PI3K and MEK inhibition.

Mouse (genetically engineered) lung adenocarcinoma model, not human patients. Kras-mutant tumors did not substantially respond to single-agent NVP-BEZ235 (a dual PI3K/mTOR inhibitor), but adding the MEK inhibitor ARRY-142886 produced marked synergy in shrinking these Kras-mutant cancers. This supports the claim that the combination is effective against KRAS-mutant tumors, within preclinical in vivo evidence only. The abstract's own conclusion is hedged ('may effectively treat'), so it does not establish clinical effectiveness in humans.

Cell-line study of KRAS-mutant pancreatic cancer. It reports synergistic cell death when ERK inhibition is combined with PI3K inhibition, which is directionally consistent, but the intervention is an ERK inhibitor rather than a MEK 1/2 inhibitor, and no tumor-level or in vivo treatment efficacy is reported. It also notes that PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling is associated with resistance to ERK inhibition. This is insufficient to assess the claim about treating KRAS-mutant tumors with PI3K plus MEK inhibitors.

Xenograft study of PI3K inhibitor PX-866 as single agent. It shows oncogenic Ras predicts resistance to PI3K inhibition, and that rational combinations may be developed, but it does not test a PI3K plus MEK combination. It neither supports nor contradicts the claim about combination efficacy in KRAS-mutant tumors.

The abstract reports that memory CD4+ T cells enhance production of multiple innate inflammatory cytokines and chemokines in the lung, and that during influenza infection this leads to early control of virus. This matches the claim's early chemokine production and early viral control in the lung. Limits: the abstract does not state the species (the study appears to be animal, not human), and it is a single study. Sentence 3 adds that the effect requires cognate antigen recognition and is independent of IFN-γ and TNF-α.

This is an in vitro study of pneumococcal infection of respiratory epithelial cells. It measures CXC chemokine responses (sentences 2 and 5) but does not measure viral infection or viral control, so it cannot assess the claim. It also reports that CbpA inhibits chemokine induction, which is about bacteria rather than viruses.

This is a mouse study of IL-10 and RSV lung inflammation. It reports chemokine expression and inflammation but does not report any measure of viral load or viral clearance. Its focus is on inflammation timing and IL-10 effects, not on whether early chemokine production improves viral control, so it neither supports nor contradicts the claim.

The abstract reports that memory CD4+ T cells enhance production of multiple innate inflammatory cytokines and chemokines in the lung, and that during influenza infection this leads to early control of virus. This matches the claim that early production of inflammatory chemokines improves viral control in the lung. The mechanism is attributed to memory CD4+ T cells, and the abstract does not explicitly frame the chemokines as the cause of control, so the support is strong but not total.

This abstract concerns CCR7-dependent egress of CD8 T cells from the influenza-infected lung and its role in retaining effectors for viral clearance. It does not measure early inflammatory chemokine production or its effect on viral control, so it neither supports nor contradicts the claim.

The abstract says the contribution of febrile seizures to later epilepsy 'has remained controversial' and does not test whether febrile seizures lower the threshold for epilepsy. In a rat model, febrile-like seizures produced a persistent increase in presynaptic inhibitory transmission in the hippocampus. That shows lasting changes in excitability but not a lowered seizure threshold or epilepsy development, and the direction of the change does not clearly fit the claim.

The abstract concerns innate immune responses (TLR4, interleukin-1) producing focal seizures and epileptiform discharges in cortex. It does not mention febrile seizures or whether they affect later epilepsy risk, so it is not relevant to the claim.

This is a rat model of hyperthermia-induced complex febrile seizures, so it is animal rather than human evidence. It reports persistent changes in hippocampal synaptic transmission (a presynaptic increase in inhibitory transmission lasting into adulthood) and says that the contribution of febrile seizures to later epilepsy 'has remained controversial.' It does not measure epilepsy development or seizure threshold, so it neither establishes nor refutes that febrile seizures lower the threshold for epilepsy.

This study concerns mTOR signaling in a kainate-induced status epilepticus rat model of temporal lobe epilepsy. It does not involve febrile seizures or seizure threshold, so it does not bear on the claim.

This study examines astrocyte-neuron interactions in NMDA-induced focal seizures in rat entorhinal cortex slices. It does not involve febrile seizures, epilepsy development, or a febrile-seizure-related threshold, so it does not address the claim.

This is a human prospective study (Million Women Study, 7610 cases, 10,196 controls) testing gene-environment interactions for 12 low-penetrance polymorphisms and 10 environmental factors. It found no significant interaction after multiple-testing correction, and the risks associated with the polymorphisms did not vary with those factors. The abstract describes environmental factors as established risk factors only as background. It does not measure the relative contribution of genetic versus non-genetic factors, so it neither supports nor contradicts the claim that development is determined exclusively by genetics.

This human systematic review and meta-analysis of 57 studies reports associations between perinatal exposures and breast cancer risk, including birthweight (RR 1.15), birth length (RR 1.28), and maternal pre-eclampsia/eclampsia (RR 0.48). Its interpretation states that the intrauterine environment contributes to the predisposition of women to breast cancer in adulthood. That is a non-genetic contributing factor, which is incompatible with the word 'exclusively' in the claim. The review reports associations, so the causal strength is not established, but the claim of exclusive genetic determination is still contradicted.

This review states that epidemiologic studies suggest ovarian hormones contribute to the development of breast cancer at all stages. It also reports that premenopausal obesity reduces risk, postmenopausal obesity and menopausal estrogen replacement therapy increase risk, and early menopause reduces risk. These are non-genetic hormonal and lifestyle contributors, which conflicts with the claim that development is determined exclusively by genetic factors. The wording 'suggest' and 'contribute' is associational and should not be read as a established causal mechanism.

The meta-analysis reports that prenatal (intrauterine) exposures are associated with adult breast cancer risk and concludes that 'the intrauterine environment contributes to the predisposition of women to breast cancer in adulthood.' This contradicts the claim that development is determined exclusively by genetic factors. Sentence 1 notes that the proposed mechanisms include non-genetic hormonal and growth factors alongside genetic or epigenetic events.

Pooled data from 32 studies show birth size (weight, length, head circumference) is positively associated with adult breast cancer risk, and the authors conclude birth length is an independent correlate of risk. This indicates non-genetic prenatal factors influence development, contradicting the claim of exclusive genetic determination. The abstract does not directly quantify the genetic contribution, so the contradiction rests on the 'exclusively' qualifier.

This study examines gene-environment interactions and reports that 12 low-penetrance polymorphisms and ten established environmental risk factors (reproductive, behavioural, anthropometric) were analysed together. It finds no significant interaction, but it does not directly state what determines breast cancer development or quantify the relative contributions of genetic and environmental factors. It therefore neither supports nor contradicts the claim of exclusive genetic determination.

In a series of 577 breast carcinomas, ALDH1 expression detected by immunostaining correlated with poor prognosis. This is the opposite of the claim that ALDH1 expression is associated with better outcomes.

This abstract studies DUSP4 deficiency and chemotherapy resistance after neoadjuvant chemotherapy. It does not measure ALDH1 expression or its association with breast cancer outcomes, so it neither supports nor contradicts the claim.

The abstract reports that in a series of 577 human breast carcinomas, ALDH1 expression detected by immunostaining correlated with poor prognosis. This is the opposite direction of the claim that ALDH1 expression is associated with better breast cancer outcomes. The study is observational (human tumor series), and the finding is a correlation, not a causal claim. Only one abstract was read; the search also returned 43385013 (normal basal breast cell lines), which was not read and was not assessed.

This is a 17-country cohort (human) comparing income groups. Major cardiovascular events were 3.99, 5.38 and 6.43 per 1000 person-years in high-, middle- and low-income countries, and case fatality was highest in low-income countries (17.3%). The claim is supported for cardiovascular disease burden, a subset of NCDs, measured as event rates and case fatality rather than prevalence. The authors also note that the risk-factor burden was lowest in low-income countries (sentence 4 and 9), so the support is for outcome burden, not for risk factors.

This is a single-country (Samoa) implementation report on a WHO NCD package in seven villages. It reports a high NCD risk prevalence (50.1%) but does not compare disease burden across economic settings, so it cannot test the claim.

This cross-national analysis links soft drink consumption to overweight, obesity and diabetes prevalence across 75 countries. It notes the associations held in low- and middle-income countries, but it does not report that NCD prevalence is higher in low-income settings than in higher-income ones, so it neither supports nor contradicts the claim.

In 17 countries, rates of major cardiovascular events and case fatality were higher in low- and middle-income countries than in high-income countries (e.g., 6.43 vs 3.99 events per 1000 person-years; case fatality 17.3% in low-income vs 6.5% in high-income). The conclusion states that CVD rates and deaths were substantially higher in low-income countries. This supports the claim for disease burden (outcomes). Note that the risk-factor burden was actually lowest in low-income countries, so the support applies to event and mortality burden rather than risk factors.

The abstract describes an NCD screening and intervention program in Samoa, a small island developing state with rising NCD morbidity and mortality. It does not compare NCD burden across economic settings, so it neither supports nor contradicts the claim that burden is higher in low-economic settings.

The abstract links soft drink consumption to overweight, obesity, and diabetes across 75 countries, and notes the findings hold in low- and middle-income countries. It does not report or compare disease burden between high- and low-income settings, so it does not directly address the claim. Income is only a control variable here.

The review states that massive mitoptosis can cause cell death through release to the cytosol of death proteins normally hidden in the intermembrane space. It does not name cytochrome c and concerns mitoptosis rather than apoptosis specifically, so it does not directly address the claim.

The abstract states that mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization, which occurs in mitochondrial-pathway apoptosis, is responsible for releasing cytochrome c and other intermembrane space proteins. This supports the claim that cytochrome c is released from the intermembrane space during apoptosis.

The abstract reports mitochondria-dependent apoptotic events in phosphate-treated vascular smooth muscle cells, including release of cytochrome c from the mitochondria into the cytosol and subsequent caspase-3 activation. This directly supports the claim.

This commentary states that apoptosis via the mitochondrial pathway involves MOMP, which is responsible for release of cytochrome c and other intermembrane space proteins. It is a review/commentary, not primary data, and it describes the mitochondrial pathway in general rather than a specific experiment, but it directly matches the claim.

This review says massive mitoptosis can cause cell death through release to cytosol of death proteins normally in the intermembrane space. However, it does not name cytochrome c and ties the release to mitoptosis rather than apoptosis, so it does not directly establish the specific claim.

This study concerns the redox state of cytochrome c and its inhibition by glutathione in neurons and cancer cells. It does not report or examine release of cytochrome c from the intermembrane space to the cytosol, so it neither supports nor contradicts the claim.

The abstract studies rapamycin in adult Drosophila melanogaster and reports life span extension, with associated resistance to starvation and paraquat, and mechanisms involving TORC1, autophagy and translation. It does not measure triacylglycerol concentrations or any lipid outcome, so it neither supports nor contradicts the claim that rapamycin decreases triacylglycerols in fruit flies.

The abstract is a double-blind placebo-controlled human trial of a fruit and vegetable juice concentrate (Juice Plus+) in Japanese subjects. It involves no rapamycin, no fruit flies, and no triacylglycerol outcome, so it is not relevant to the claim.

The abstract shows that feeding rapamycin to adult Drosophila extends lifespan via TORC1, affecting autophagy and translation, and increases resistance to starvation and paraquat. It does not mention triacylglycerol or whole-body lipid levels, so it neither supports nor contradicts the claim that rapamycin decreases triacylglycerol concentration in flies.

The abstract reports serial in vivo imaging of podocyte motility. After unilateral ureteral ligation (an injury model), podocytes formed multicellular clusters and migrated into Bowman's capsule, and simultaneous migration of multiple podocytes was observed. This supports the claim that podocytes are motile and migrate in the presence of injury.

The abstract covers podocyte integrin beta1 and ILK signaling in normal glomerular development and filtration. It does not address podocyte motility or migration, nor any injury model, so it neither supports nor contradicts the claim.

This is a mouse in vivo study. Serial multiphoton imaging showed podocyte motility, and after unilateral ureteral ligation (an injury model) podocytes formed clusters and migrated into the parietal Bowman's capsule. Tracking revealed simultaneous migration of multiple podocytes. This supports the claim in mice after injury. It does not establish the claim for human podocytes, and the authors describe the findings as supporting a dynamic glomerular environment rather than stating a general mechanism.

This study of cultured human podocytes examines basement membrane components, podocalyxin expression, adhesion and spreading, and morphology. It does not measure podocyte motility or migration, and it does not involve injury in vivo.

This study links TRPC6 mutations to familial focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and describes slit diaphragm channel function. It does not address podocyte motility or migration in response to injury.

The abstract proposes a 'charge zipper' model for folding and self-assembly of the TatA pore (salt bridges between an amphiphilic helix and a densely charged region), supported by molecular dynamics and charge-mutant experiments. It does not mention TatAd complexes, Class 1 complexes, arm density, or any structural rearrangement that accounts for arm density. The claim's specific population and outcome are not addressed.

The abstract studies purified TatABC complexes from E. coli, Salmonella typhimurium and Agrobacterium tumefaciens. It reports stain-excluding densities around central pools in single-particle EM, but does not mention TatAd, Class 1 complexes, arm density, or a charge zipper mechanism, and does not link any density to structural rearrangements. The organisms and complex type do not match the claim.

The abstract describes B. subtilis TatAd and TatAdCd complexes, including a discrete ~270 kDa TatAd complex by gel filtration. It does not report arm density, Class 1 classification, structural rearrangements, or a charge zipper mechanism, so it neither supports nor contradicts the claim.

The abstract proposes a 'charge zipper' model for folding and self-assembly of the TatA pore (salt bridges between an amphiphilic helix and a charged region), and suggests it may apply to other membrane proteins. It does not mention arm density, TatAd complexes, Class 1 TatAd complexes, or structural rearrangements that would produce arm density. The claim's causal link is therefore not addressed.

The abstract reports single-particle EM of purified TatABC complexes from three bacteria, noting stain-excluding densities and size variation consistent with modular assembly. It does not mention arm density, TatAd complexes, Class 1 classification, or a charge zipper mechanism, so it neither supports nor contradicts the claim.

The abstract characterizes a discrete approximately 270 kDa TatAd complex in B. subtilis and a TatAdCd complex, and notes the singular nature of TatAd. It does not describe arm density, Class 1 TatAd complexes, structural rearrangements, or a charge zipper mechanism, so it does not address the claim.

The systematic review of RCTs of community screening for impaired vision in adults aged 65+ found that adding a visual screening component did not improve self-reported visual problems (pooled OR 1.04, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.22), and concluded that screening asymptomatic older people is not justified on present evidence. This supports the claim. Caveat: outcomes were self-reported rather than measured visual acuity, and the authors note a small reduction (11%) cannot be excluded.

The abstract is a systematic review of RCTs of community population screening for impaired vision in adults aged 65 or over. Pooled across five multiphasic-assessment trials (3494 people), including a visual screening component did not result in improvements in self-reported visual problems (pooled OR 1.04, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.22). The authors conclude that screening of asymptomatic older people in the community is not justified on present evidence. Qualifications: no trials primarily assessed visual screening, all outcomes were self-reported, and a small 11% reduction cannot be excluded. The claim concerns 'improved vision', while the outcome was self-reported visual problems, so the match is close but not exact.

This observational study compares fear of falling in glaucoma patients with visual field loss against controls. It does not evaluate asymptomatic visual impairment screening or whether screening improves vision, so it neither supports nor contradicts the claim.

In an experimental autoimmune myocarditis model (BALB/c mice immunized with cardiac alpha-myosin heavy chain peptide), IFN-gamma receptor-deficient mice developed severe myocarditis with high mortality and persistent disease, the opposite of resistance. The authors conclude IFN-gamma protects against lethal myocarditis.

In murine experimental autoimmune myocarditis induced by cardiac myosin immunization, lack of IFN-gamma (by antibody depletion or genetic deficiency) exacerbated myocarditis, and the authors state IFN-gamma plays a protective role. This is incompatible with IFN-gamma-deficient mice being highly resistant. The same abstract reports that IL-12Rbeta1- and STAT4-deficient mice were resistant, but that is a different genotype than the claim.

In autoimmune myocarditis in mice, IFN-gamma-deficient mice developed fatal autoimmune disease, and IFN-gamma production limits disease progression. This contradicts the claim of resistance in IFN-gamma-deficient mice. The abstract reports resistance only in IL-12p40-deficient mice, which is a different genotype.

IFN-gamma receptor-deficient mice developed severe myocarditis with high mortality and persistent disease, and the authors conclude IFN-gamma protects against lethal autoimmune myocarditis. This is the opposite of resistance.

IFN-gamma-deficient mice developed fatal autoimmune disease, and IFN-gamma production limits disease progression. The claim that IFN-gamma-deficient mice are highly resistant is contradicted. The abstract's resistance finding concerns IL-12p40-deficient mice, not IFN-gamma-deficient mice.
IFN-gamma suppresses experimental autoimmune myocarditis. Lack of IFN-gamma through antibody depletion or genetic deficiency exacerbated myocarditis, so IFN-gamma-deficient mice are not resistant.
